modules.title: How experts get to the frontier
modules.summary: The common skills of going deep: choosing a specialty, reading papers, engineering feedback, finding community, and writing to learn.

lessons.title: Choosing a specialty: interest x leverage x market
lessons.objective: By the end you can score 3 candidate specialties on interest, leverage and market and pick one to go deep on.
concept: After broad foundations, the question changes from "what can I learn next?" to "where do I go deep?". Becoming one of the best in the world is only achievable in a **narrow** area, because depth compounds: the thousandth hour on compilers teaches you more than the first hour on a new field. The cost of narrowing is real too, so you want to choose on evidence, not mood. A useful screen multiplies three factors: **interest** (will you still care at hour 3,000?), **leverage** (does skill here make everything else you do more valuable?), and **market** (does the world pay for or need this?).

Score each candidate 1-5 on the three axes and **multiply**, not add. Multiplication punishes a zero: a field you love with no market (interest 5, market 1) scores low, and so does a lucrative field you will quit in a month. Leverage is the axis beginners ignore: compilers, ML, security and performance all make you better at *everything else you build*, which is why they are good specialties even if a specific job market dips. Write the numbers down. The act of committing a guess to paper turns a vague feeling into a claim you can revisit in six months.
lessons.tryit: Pick three specialties you are actually considering (e.g. compilers, ML, security). Make a 3-column table and score each 1-5 on interest, leverage, market. Multiply the row. Write one sentence on why the winner won.

questions.prompt: Why does the screen multiply the three scores instead of adding them?
options: A single near-zero factor should sink the whole choice
questions.explain: Multiplying means any factor near 1 drags the product down, capturing the real-world truth that a field you will quit, or one nobody needs, is a bad bet regardless of the other scores. Adding lets one high score hide a fatal zero.

questions.prompt: Specialty A scores interest 5, leverage 2, market 2. Specialty B scores interest 3, leverage 4, market 3. Which does the screen prefer and by how much?
questions.explain: A = 5*2*2 = 20. B = 3*4*3 = 36. B wins. Note B wins despite lower interest because its leverage and market are balanced and higher-product.

questions.prompt: A friend argues 'just pick the highest-paying field and interest will follow.' What is the strongest counter grounded in this lesson's model?
options: Interest near zero collapses the product; you will stall before reaching world-class depth
Markets never change so pay is irrelevant
questions.explain: The model's whole point is that reaching the frontier takes thousands of hours; if interest is near 1 the product collapses and you quit long before depth compounds, so pay never materialises. The counter is not that pay is unpredictable but that low interest is a multiplicative killer.

questions.prompt: Which axis do beginners most often ignore, per the lesson?
questions.explain: Leverage, whether the skill makes everything else you build more valuable, is the axis beginners overlook; it is why compilers/ML/security/performance are strong picks.

lessons.title: Reading research papers: the three-pass method
lessons.objective: By the end you can apply Keshav's three-pass method to decide in five minutes whether a paper is worth a deep read.
concept: World-class practitioners read the primary literature, not just blog summaries, because the frontier lives in papers first. The problem is that a paper read linearly, start to finish, is slow and demoralising. Keshav's **three-pass method** fixes this. **Pass 1** (5-10 min): read the title, abstract, introduction, section headings and conclusion; ignore everything else. You now know the category, context, and claimed contributions, and can decide whether to continue. Most papers stop here, which is the point: triage protects your hours.

**Pass 2** (up to 1 hour): read the whole paper but skip proofs. Study the figures and tables carefully, since a good paper's story is in its graphs, and mark references you should chase. After pass 2 you can summarise the paper's thrust to someone else. **Pass 3** is for papers you must master or implement: you virtually re-create the work, re-deriving results and questioning every assumption, which can take many hours. The discipline is matching effort to value: three cheap passes let you read ten papers to find the one that earns a pass 3.
lessons.tryit: Pick a classic paper in your chosen specialty (e.g. 'Attention Is All You Need'). Do a timed 10-minute pass 1 only. Write down the category, the main contributions as you understood them, and one question you would need pass 2 to answer.

questions.prompt: In Keshav's method, what do you read during pass 1?
questions.explain: Pass 1 is a 5-10 minute scan of title, abstract, introduction, section headings and conclusion to categorise the paper and decide whether to go on. Proofs and full body are later passes.

questions.prompt: You have 2 hours and a stack of 8 unfamiliar papers for a literature review. What does the method suggest?
options: Read the first paper in full, ignore the rest
Pass 1 all 8, then pass 2 the 2-3 that survive
questions.explain: Triage first: a quick pass 1 on all eight (under 90 min total) identifies the two or three worth a pass 2 in the remaining time. Deep-reading the first paper wastes your budget on possibly-irrelevant work.

questions.prompt: A paper's pass-2 figures seem to contradict its abstract's headline claim. What is the disciplined response?
options: Trust the abstract; figures are decorative
Escalate to pass 3 on the relevant section to re-derive and judge the claim
Email the authors before reading further
questions.explain: An apparent contradiction between figures and claims is exactly the signal that this paper needs a pass 3 on that section: re-derive the result and test the assumption. Blindly trusting either the abstract or discarding wastes the signal.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of stopping most papers after pass 1?
options: To protect your limited reading hours via triage
Pass 1 is the only legal way to read
questions.explain: Triage: cheap passes let you survey many papers and spend deep effort only on the few that earn it.

steps.label: Pass 1 (5-10m)
steps.detail: Title, abstract, intro, headings, conclusion. Decide: continue?

steps.label: Pass 2 (<=1h)
steps.detail: Full read, skip proofs. Study figures. Can now summarise it.

steps.label: Pass 3 (hours)
steps.detail: Virtually re-implement. Re-derive, question every assumption.

lessons.title: Building a deliberate-practice loop with feedback
lessons.objective: By the end you can design a weekly practice loop that targets a specific weakness and produces feedback you can act on.
concept: Ten thousand hours of *playing* does not make an expert; ten thousand hours of **deliberate practice** does. Deliberate practice, in Ericsson's sense, has four features: it targets a **specific** sub-skill just beyond your current ability, it is **effortful** and not much fun, it produces **immediate feedback**, and you **repeat with correction**. Mindless repetition of what you already do well, grinding easy LeetCode, shipping the same CRUD app, builds hours but not skill. The hard part is manufacturing feedback when no coach is standing over you.

You engineer your own feedback. In code, feedback sources include failing tests you write first, a profiler's numbers, a diff against an expert's solution, code review from someone better than you, and your own predictions checked against reality (predict the output, then run it). The loop is: pick one weakness, design a drill that isolates it, attempt it at the edge of your ability, compare against ground truth, note the gap, and adjust the next drill. Keeping a short log of weakness -> drill -> gap turns vague effort into a visible curve.
lessons.tryit: Name one concrete weakness in your chosen specialty (e.g. 'I cannot write a recursive-descent parser without peeking'). Design a 30-minute drill that isolates it and defines its feedback source. Run the drill once and log the gap you observed.

questions.prompt: Which four features define deliberate practice?
options: Specific target, effortful, immediate feedback, repeat-with-correction
Long hours, many topics, no breaks, memorisation
questions.explain: Ericsson's definition: a specific sub-skill at the edge of ability, effortful, with immediate feedback, repeated with correction. The other options describe passive or unfocused study.

questions.prompt: You want to improve at systems debugging but keep re-solving bugs you already understand. What change makes this deliberate practice?
options: Solve more bugs of the same kind
Pick bugs one level harder than you can currently handle and compare your diagnosis to the real root cause
Read a debugging book cover to cover
questions.explain: Deliberate practice must sit just beyond current ability and produce feedback: harder-than-comfortable bugs plus a check of your diagnosis against the true root cause. Re-solving familiar bugs adds hours but not skill.

questions.prompt: A learner with no mentor says 'deliberate practice is impossible alone because it needs a coach for feedback.' What is the best rebuttal?
options: Feedback can be engineered from tests, profilers, expert diffs, and checked predictions
questions.explain: The lesson's key move is manufacturing feedback without a coach: first-written failing tests, profiler numbers, diffs against expert solutions, and predict-then-run all provide immediate ground truth. The claim that it is impossible alone ignores these sources.

questions.prompt: Why is grinding easy problems you already solve well NOT deliberate practice?
options: It is not at the edge of your ability, so it builds hours but not skill
questions.explain: Deliberate practice must target a sub-skill just beyond current ability; comfortable repetition accumulates hours without moving the skill frontier.

steps.label: Target
steps.detail: One specific weakness at the edge of ability

steps.label: Feedback
steps.detail: Tests, profiler, expert diff, checked prediction

steps.label: Correct
steps.detail: Note the gap; adjust next drill

lessons.title: Finding mentors and communities
lessons.objective: By the end you can identify and make a useful first contact with a mentor or community in your specialty.
concept: Depth is faster in the company of people ahead of you. A **mentor** compresses years of trial and error into a sentence of feedback; a **community** gives you a steady stream of problems, standards, and people to measure against. You rarely get this by asking a stranger to 'be my mentor', which is a large, vague request. Instead you earn attention by doing visible work: contributing a bug fix to their project, writing a thoughtful question that shows you did the reading, or publishing something they find useful.

Communities in deep technical fields tend to cluster around artefacts: open-source repos and their issue trackers, specialist Discords and mailing lists, conference talks, and reading groups. The highest-leverage move for a beginner-to-intermediate is the **good question**: one that states what you tried, what you expected, and the exact point of confusion, which is respectful of the expert's time and often answered generously. Over months, consistent small contributions turn you from a stranger into a known quantity, and mentorship follows from that relationship rather than from a cold request.
lessons.tryit: Find one real community for your specialty (a specific repo, Discord, or mailing list). Draft a single 'good question' using the structure: what I'm trying to do, what I tried, what I expected, where exactly I'm stuck. Do not send it yet; just write it.

questions.prompt: According to the lesson, how do you most reliably earn a mentor's attention?
options: Ask them directly to be your mentor
Do visible useful work and ask good questions
questions.explain: Mentorship follows from a relationship built on visible, useful work and well-formed questions, not from a cold 'be my mentor' request, which is a large vague ask.

questions.prompt: Which message is the 'good question' the lesson recommends?
options: 'Why doesn't my parser work? Code attached.'
'I'm building a Pratt parser; I expected 2+3*4 to give 14 but get 20. I think my binding powers for * are wrong, here's the table. Where's my error?'
questions.explain: The good question states the goal, what was tried, the expected vs actual result, and the precise point of confusion, which respects the expert's time and is answerable. The others are vague or dump the problem without context.

questions.prompt: You've lurked in a specialist community for weeks and want to go from stranger to known quantity. What strategy best fits the lesson?
options: Post a long introduction about yourself
Make a series of small, visible contributions (bug fixes, useful answers) over time
Ask the most famous member to review your whole project
questions.explain: Consistent small visible contributions over months build the relationship that turns you into a known quantity; a self-intro or a big cold ask does not. This mirrors earning mentorship through visible work.

questions.prompt: What does a mentor primarily compress for you?
options: Years of trial and error into targeted feedback
questions.explain: A mentor's value is compressing their accumulated trial-and-error into a sentence of feedback that would otherwise cost you years.

resource.title: Julia Evans, How to ask good questions

lessons.title: Writing to learn: technical blogging
lessons.objective: By the end you can turn something you just learned into a short, honest technical blog post that deepens your own understanding.
concept: Writing is not just output; it is a **learning tool**. When you explain a mechanism in prose, gaps you glossed over become impossible to hide: you cannot write a clear sentence about something you only half-understand. This is the Feynman effect, and it is why strong practitioners blog even when few read it. A good learning post is small and honest: it takes one concrete thing you figured out this week, shows the real code or the real confusion, and explains it to a reader who is one step behind you.

Structure that works: open with the concrete problem or question, show the thing (code, a trace, a diagram), explain why it works including the part that confused you, and end with what you'd check next. Avoid the two failure modes: the summary that just restates a tutorial (no learning, no reader value) and the grand overview that hides that you don't actually understand the details. A post that admits 'I was confused by X until I realised Y' is both better writing and better learning than one pretending mastery.
lessons.tryit: Take one thing you learned this week in your specialty. Write a 300-400 word post using the structure: concrete problem, show it, explain why (including what confused you), what's next. Publish it or save it as a draft you could publish.

questions.prompt: Why does the lesson call writing a 'learning tool', not just output?
options: Explaining in prose exposes gaps you can't write clearly about
questions.explain: The Feynman effect: you cannot write a clear sentence about something you only half-understand, so writing forces the gaps into the open. Revenue and employer demands are not the lesson's point.

questions.prompt: Which post is most likely to teach its author the most, per the lesson?
options: A 2000-word overview of all of machine learning
A 350-word post walking through the one bug that broke the author's backprop and the fix
A list of links with no commentary
A restatement of an official tutorial
questions.explain: A small, concrete, honest post about one real thing (the backprop bug and fix) forces the author to understand the details. Grand overviews and tutorial restatements let you hide gaps and teach little.

questions.prompt: A learner says 'I shouldn't blog until I'm an expert, or I'll post something wrong.' Evaluate this against the lesson.
options: Writing for a reader one step behind you is where most of the learning happens; honest uncertainty is a feature, not a disqualifier
You should only blog after 10,000 hours
questions.explain: The lesson's model is explicitly to write for someone one step behind and to admit confusion ('I was stuck on X until Y'), which both teaches and is good writing. Waiting for expertise removes the learning benefit entirely.

questions.prompt: What are the two failure modes of a learning post the lesson names?
options: Restating a tutorial, and a grand overview that hides missing details
questions.explain: The two failure modes are the tutorial restatement (no learning/value) and the grand overview that conceals that the author does not understand the details.

steps.detail: The concrete question or bug you hit

steps.label: Explain why
steps.detail: Including the part that confused you

steps.label: What's next
steps.detail: The open question you'd check next

project.title: Paper-reading journal (10 papers) + first blog post
project.brief: Build the habit infrastructure for the whole stage: a journal of ten papers read with the three-pass method and one published blog post. This turns the frontier skills from theory into a repeatable loop you own.
milestones: Pick your specialty with the interest x leverage x market table and write the one-sentence rationale
Create a journal; for each of 10 papers record pass-1 category/contribution and whether it earned pass 2
Do a full pass 2 on at least 3 of the papers, with figures summarised in your own words
Identify one real community and draft one 'good question' using the four-part structure
Write and publish one 300-400 word learning post about something a paper taught you
project.stretch: Do a full pass 3 on one paper by re-implementing its core result in code.

exam.prompt: You have 3 hours to survey 10 papers for a new project. Which plan best matches the three-pass method?
options: Pass 1 all 10, then pass 2 the 3 that survive
Read only the 10 abstracts and stop
exam.explain: Triage with pass 1 across all ten, then invest pass 2 in the survivors. Deep-reading two or reading all ten fully both blow the budget.

exam.prompt: Rank the leverage of choosing to specialise in compilers for a backend engineer, using this module's model.
options: High: compiler knowledge improves how you reason about every language and tool you use
exam.explain: Leverage asks whether the skill makes everything else more valuable; compiler understanding changes how you read, debug and optimise all code, so it is high-leverage even if compiler jobs are few.

exam.prompt: Your practice log shows 40 hours this month but no measurable improvement. Which lesson's idea most directly diagnoses the problem?
options: Deliberate practice: hours without edge-of-ability targeting and feedback don't build skill
exam.explain: Hours without deliberate practice (specific target, feedback, correction) accumulate time but not skill, which is exactly this symptom.

exam.prompt: Connect to your earlier foundations: you already know data structures and algorithms. How should that change how you pick a specialty here?
options: Prior foundations raise the leverage of specialties that build on them, and let you start practice at a harder edge
It means you should avoid anything algorithmic
It guarantees you'll reach world-class faster
exam.explain: Existing foundations increase leverage for adjacent specialties and let you set the deliberate-practice edge higher; they neither guarantee speed nor should be ignored.

exam.prompt: What is the single best way to earn mentorship according to the module?
options: Visible useful work plus well-formed questions
exam.explain: Mentorship follows a relationship built on visible contributions and good questions, not a cold ask.

exam.prompt: Which blog post best serves learning, per the module?
options: A broad survey of your whole field
A short honest walkthrough of one thing you just figured out, confusion included
exam.explain: Small, concrete, honest posts for a reader one step behind force real understanding; surveys and restatements hide gaps.

exam.prompt: A specialty scores interest 5, leverage 5, market 1. A mentor says 'the market will come, just build.' Should you commit years to it based on this module?
options: Yes, interest and leverage are enough
Be cautious: the product is low (25) because market ~1; treat the mentor's claim as a hypothesis to test, not a reason to ignore the screen
No, never enter a low-market field
exam.explain: Multiplication makes the near-1 market factor dominate (5*5*1=25). The disciplined response is to treat 'the market will come' as a testable hypothesis, not to override the screen or to rule the field out forever.

modules.title: Track: Compilers and languages
modules.summary: Build a language end to end: lexing, parsing, ASTs, a bytecode VM, closures and garbage collection.

lessons.title: Lexing: turning characters into tokens
lessons.objective: By the end you can write a scanner that converts a source string into a stream of typed tokens.
concept: A compiler or interpreter runs in stages, and the first is **lexing** (also called scanning or tokenising). The lexer reads the raw character stream and groups it into **tokens**: the smallest meaningful units, like the number `12`, the operator `+`, the identifier `foo`, or a string literal. A token typically carries a type, the matched text (its lexeme), and a source position for error messages. Lexing throws away noise, whitespace and comments, so the parser never has to think about individual characters.

The classic lexer is a loop with a cursor over the input. At each position it looks at the current character and decides which token it begins: a digit starts a number (keep consuming digits), a letter starts an identifier or keyword (consume alphanumerics, then check a keyword table), a quote starts a string. This is the **maximal munch** rule: match the longest token you can, which is why `==` lexes as one token, not two `=`. Regular expressions can express each token class, and tools like `re` or lex/flex generate scanners, but hand-writing one teaches the mechanics.
lessons.tryit: Write a small Python lexer for arithmetic that turns '12 + 3*4' into a list of (type, text) tuples for NUMBER, PLUS, STAR. Handle multi-digit numbers and skip spaces. Test it on '100*2+5'.

questions.prompt: What is a token?
options: A whole line of source code
The smallest meaningful unit (number, operator, identifier) with a type and lexeme
questions.explain: A token is the smallest meaningful lexical unit, carrying a type, its matched text (lexeme), and usually a position. A line is many tokens; machine instructions come much later.

questions.prompt: The lexer uses this regex to split arithmetic. What does it print?
questions.explain: `\d+` matches maximal runs of digits so '12' stays together (maximal munch), while the single-char alternatives match '+' and '*'. findall returns the matches left to right as a list of strings.

questions.prompt: Why does maximal munch make the lexer treat '==' as one token instead of two '=' tokens?
options: Because the lexer matches the longest valid token starting at the cursor
Because the parser rejects two '=' in a row
Because regex is greedy by accident
questions.explain: Maximal munch is the deliberate rule: at each position, take the longest token that matches, so '==' is consumed as one operator. It is a design choice, not an accident of regex, and '=' alone is usually legal (assignment).

questions.prompt: What does the lexer typically discard?
questions.explain: Whitespace and comments are noise for the parser, so the lexer drops them while keeping meaningful tokens.

example.explain: A tiny lexer: strip spaces, then findall grabs maximal digit runs or a single operator, left to right, giving ['12','+','3','*','4'].

lessons.title: Parsing: recursive descent and Pratt
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain how recursive descent encodes grammar rules as functions and how Pratt parsing handles operator precedence.
concept: Parsing turns a flat token stream into a tree that reflects structure. **Recursive descent** is the most direct technique: each grammar rule becomes a function, and a rule that references another rule calls that function. For arithmetic you might have `expression -> term (('+'|'-') term)*` and `term -> factor (('*'|'/') factor)*`. Because `term` binds tighter than `expression`, and the grammar nests them accordingly, precedence falls out of the call structure for free: `2 + 3 * 4` parses with the multiplication deeper in the tree.

Writing one function per precedence level gets tedious as operators multiply. **Pratt parsing** (top-down operator precedence) is a cleaner approach for expressions: each operator token gets a **binding power** (a precedence number), and a single loop keeps consuming operators while their left binding power exceeds the current threshold. Prefix operators (unary minus, literals) and infix operators are handled by small per-token functions. Pratt parsing is what many real languages and the book Crafting Interpreters use, because it handles precedence and associativity with one elegant loop instead of a tower of functions.
lessons.tryit: On paper, draw the parse tree for '2 + 3 * 4' under the grammar expression->term(('+')term)*, term->factor(('*')factor)*. Confirm the '*' is deeper than the '+'. Then write the recursive-descent function 'term' in pseudocode.

questions.prompt: In recursive descent, what does each grammar rule become?
questions.explain: Recursive descent maps each grammar rule to a function; rule references become function calls, so the call stack mirrors the grammar.

questions.prompt: Arrange a recursive-descent 'factor' that parses a number or a parenthesised expression.
questions.explain: You must check for '(' before advancing past it, then parse the inner expression, then expect the closing ')', then return that node; the number() fallback is the last line. Each step depends on the previous, so the order is forced.

questions.prompt: Why does '2 + 3 * 4' evaluate to 14 rather than 20 under the given grammar?
options: Because 'term' (handling '*') nests deeper than 'expression' (handling '+'), so 3*4 is a subtree computed first
questions.explain: Precedence comes from grammar nesting: expression calls term, so the '*' subtree (3*4=12) sits below the '+', giving 2+12=14. Lexing and munch do not reorder operators.

questions.prompt: In Pratt parsing, what role does an operator's binding power play?
options: It is a precedence number; the loop keeps consuming operators while their binding power exceeds the current threshold
questions.explain: Binding power is the precedence number that drives Pratt's single loop: higher-binding operators grab their operands first, encoding precedence and associativity without one function per level.

left.title: Recursive descent
points: Simple but verbose for many operators

lessons.title: ASTs and tree-walking interpreters
lessons.objective: By the end you can represent a program as an AST and evaluate it by walking the tree recursively.
concept: The parser's output is an **abstract syntax tree (AST)**: a tree where each node is a language construct (a binary operation, a number literal, an if-statement) and children are its parts. It is 'abstract' because it drops syntactic noise like parentheses and keeps only structure. A `2 + 3 * 4` AST has a `+` node whose right child is a `*` node; the tree itself encodes precedence, so evaluation needs no further knowledge of operator rules.

A **tree-walking interpreter** executes the program by recursively walking the AST. Evaluation is a function `eval(node)` that branches on node type: a number node returns its value, a binary-op node evaluates both children and applies the operator, an if-node evaluates its condition then one branch. This is the simplest way to run a language and is how Crafting Interpreters' first interpreter (jlox) works. It is slow, because every operation re-dispatches on node type, which motivates the bytecode VM in the next lesson, but it is wonderfully clear.
lessons.tryit: Define an AST for arithmetic as nested tuples, e.g. ('add', ('num', 2), ('mul', ('num', 3), ('num', 4))). Write eval(node) handling 'num', 'add', 'mul'. Confirm it returns 14 for that tree.

questions.prompt: What makes a syntax tree 'abstract'?
options: It drops syntactic noise (like parentheses) and keeps only structure
questions.explain: An AST abstracts away surface syntax such as parentheses and keeps the essential structure; precedence is baked into the shape, not into stored punctuation.

questions.prompt: Arrange a tree-walking evaluator for numbers and addition nodes.
questions.explain: The function header comes first, then the base case checking for a 'num' node and returning its value, then the recursive case that evaluates both children and adds them. The base case must precede the recursive return, so the order is unique.

questions.prompt: What does this tree-walking evaluator print?
questions.explain: The outer 'add' evaluates its children: ('num',2) gives 2, and the inner ('add',('num',3),('num',4)) gives 3+4=7. So 2+7=9. The tree shape determines the order of evaluation.

questions.prompt: Why is a tree-walking interpreter typically slower than a bytecode VM?
options: It uses more memory for tokens
Every operation re-dispatches on node type during the walk, adding overhead per node
It re-lexes the source each step
questions.explain: Tree walking pays a type-dispatch and pointer-chasing cost at every node on every execution; compiling to bytecode flattens this into a tight instruction loop, which is why VMs are faster.

example.explain: eval branches on the node tag and recurses into children; the tree's shape gives 3*4=12 then 2+12=14.

lessons.title: Bytecode virtual machines
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain how a compiler emits bytecode and how a stack-based VM executes it.
concept: To run faster than a tree walker, compilers emit **bytecode**: a flat sequence of compact instructions for a virtual machine you define. Most teaching VMs (including Crafting Interpreters' clox and CPython) are **stack machines**. Instructions push and pop operands on an operand stack: `OP_CONSTANT 2` pushes 2, `OP_CONSTANT 3` pushes 3, `OP_ADD` pops two and pushes their sum. There are no registers to allocate; the stack is the scratch space, which keeps the instruction set tiny and the compiler simple.

The VM is a loop: fetch the next opcode, decode it, execute it, repeat (the fetch-decode-execute cycle). Compiling `2 + 3 * 4` yields, in postfix order, push 2, push 3, push 4, multiply, add, because the compiler emits children before the operator (a post-order walk of the AST). This flattening is why VMs are fast: the hot loop is a tight switch over byte opcodes with no tree pointers to chase. The trade-off is a compile step and a less readable program representation.
lessons.tryit: By hand, write the bytecode (as a list of ops) for '2 + 3 * 4' for a stack VM with OP_CONST, OP_ADD, OP_MUL. Then trace the operand stack after each instruction and confirm the final value is 14.

questions.prompt: In a stack-based VM, where do instructions get their operands?
questions.explain: Stack machines push and pop operands on an operand stack; OP_ADD pops two values and pushes the sum. There are no registers to allocate, which keeps the design simple.

questions.prompt: What is the correct bytecode (operand order) for 2 + 3 * 4 on a stack VM?
questions.explain: A post-order walk emits operands before operators: push 2, 3, 4, then MUL (3*4=12) leaves [2,12], then ADD leaves [14]. The multiplication must be emitted before the addition to respect precedence.
questions.code: stack VM ops: CONST n, ADD, MUL

questions.prompt: Why does flattening an AST into bytecode usually run faster than walking the tree?
options: The VM's hot loop is a tight switch over bytes with no tree-node dispatch or pointer chasing
questions.explain: The tree walker dispatches on node type and chases child pointers per node; bytecode becomes a linear instruction stream executed by a tight fetch-decode-execute switch, which the CPU handles much faster.

questions.prompt: Name the VM's core loop.
questions.explain: The VM repeatedly fetches the next opcode, decodes it, and executes it: the fetch-decode-execute cycle.

lessons.title: Closures and garbage collection
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain how closures capture their environment and how a mark-sweep garbage collector reclaims unreachable memory.
concept: A **closure** is a function together with the environment it captured when it was created. When an inner function references a variable from an enclosing scope, the language must keep that variable alive even after the outer function returns, so the variable is stored in a heap-allocated environment the closure points to. In Python this is why a counter factory works: each call to the factory creates a fresh captured cell, and the returned inner function reads and updates that cell via `nonlocal`. Implementing closures in an interpreter means your values are no longer just numbers; functions carry environment pointers.

Once you heap-allocate environments and objects, you need **garbage collection** to reclaim what is no longer reachable, or you leak memory. The classic teaching algorithm is **mark-sweep**: starting from the roots (the stack, globals), mark every object reachable by following pointers; then sweep the heap and free everything unmarked. Crafting Interpreters implements exactly this for clox. The key definition is **reachability**, not whether a value is 'used again' in some human sense, the collector can only see what is reachable from roots, so an object no root can reach is garbage even if it was important a moment ago.
lessons.tryit: Write a Python make_counter() that returns an inner function incrementing a captured count via nonlocal. Create two independent counters and show they don't share state. Then, on paper, draw which objects a mark-sweep GC would mark as reachable if you drop one counter.

questions.prompt: What is a closure?
options: A function bundled with the environment it captured at creation
questions.explain: A closure pairs a function with the captured variables from its enclosing scope, which must be kept alive (on the heap) after the outer function returns.

questions.prompt: What does this closure-based counter print?
questions.code:
def make_counter():
    c = 0
    def inc():
        nonlocal c
        c += 1
        return c
    return inc
f = make_counter()
print(f(), f(), f())
questions.explain: `inc` captures the cell `c`; `nonlocal` lets it rebind that captured variable. Three calls increment the same captured cell to 1, then 2, then 3. A fresh make_counter() would start over at its own cell.

questions.prompt: A mark-sweep collector runs. An object X was heavily used a moment ago but no root can now reach it. What happens to X?
options: It is kept because it was recently used
It is swept (freed) because the collector only keeps reachable objects
It is marked but not swept
questions.explain: Mark-sweep defines garbage by reachability from roots, not recency of use. If no root reaches X, it is unmarked in the mark phase and freed in the sweep. Recency is irrelevant to correctness here.

questions.prompt: Why must a closure's captured variable live on the heap rather than the outer function's stack frame?
options: The outer frame is destroyed when it returns, but the closure may outlive it and still need the variable
questions.explain: Once the outer function returns its stack frame is gone; a closure that outlives it must find the captured variable somewhere persistent, so it is stored in a heap-allocated environment the closure references.

items.label: GC roots
items.detail: f -> inc -> env keeps c reachable; dropping f makes env garbage

project.title: A complete interpreter for a small language
project.brief: Implement an interpreter for a small but real language (variables, arithmetic, if/while, functions, closures). Following Crafting Interpreters, go from source text to running programs so every stage of this module becomes working code you own.
milestones: Write a lexer producing a token stream with types and positions
Write a parser (recursive descent or Pratt) that builds an AST with correct precedence
Write a tree-walking evaluator for expressions, variables, and control flow
Add functions and closures with a heap-allocated environment
Either compile to bytecode for a stack VM, or add a mark-sweep GC
project.stretch: Add first-class functions returning closures and benchmark the tree-walker against a bytecode VM on a recursive fibonacci.

exam.prompt: Trace 2+3*4 through the pipeline: which stage first makes 3*4 bind tighter than the +?
options: The parser, via grammar nesting / binding power
exam.explain: Precedence is decided by the parser: grammar nesting (or Pratt binding power) puts 3*4 in a deeper subtree. The lexer only produces tokens; the VM merely executes the order the parser fixed.

exam.prompt: You add '**' (exponent, right-associative, higher than '*'). Which parsing approach adapts with the least new code?
options: Recursive descent: add another precedence-level function
Pratt: give '**' a higher binding power and right-associativity in its infix handler
exam.explain: Pratt parsing encodes precedence and associativity as per-operator binding powers, so adding '**' is a small change to one handler; recursive descent needs an extra function per level. Lexing and evaluation strategy are unrelated.

exam.prompt: What does this closure code print?
exam.explain: adder(5) returns a closure capturing n=5; calling it with x=10 returns 10+5=15. The captured n lives on even though adder has returned.

exam.prompt: Your stack VM crashes on 'OP_ADD' with an empty stack after running compiled '2 +'. What is the real cause?
options: The parser accepted an incomplete expression and emitted an ADD with too few operands
exam.explain: A trailing '+' is a parse error; if the parser doesn't reject it, the compiler emits an OP_ADD that pops two operands when only one was pushed, underflowing the stack. The bug is upstream in parsing, not in GC or lexing.

exam.prompt: What is the output of the lexer stage?
exam.explain: Lexing produces a stream of tokens; the parser turns tokens into an AST.

exam.prompt: Connect to the ML track idea of 'dispatch cost': why might a bytecode VM beat a tree-walker for the same program, and how does this echo data-oriented design from the performance track?
options: Flattening the tree into a linear instruction stream removes per-node pointer chasing and type dispatch, improving locality just as data-oriented layouts do
exam.explain: Both ideas trade pointer-heavy tree/object graphs for flat, cache-friendly sequences the CPU streams through, reducing dispatch and improving locality. This is the same principle as data-oriented design in the performance track.

exam.prompt: After an outer function returns, its closure still reads a captured variable. Which two mechanisms from this module make that safe?
options: Heap-allocated environments plus a garbage collector that keeps them alive while reachable
exam.explain: The captured variable lives in a heap environment (so it survives the outer frame), and the GC keeps that environment alive exactly as long as the closure (a root) can reach it.

modules.summary: From tensors and hand-computed backprop to training loops, language models, and transformers.

lessons.title: Tensors and gradients
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain what a tensor is and what a gradient tells you about how to change inputs to decrease a loss.
concept: A **tensor** is just an n-dimensional array of numbers: a scalar is a 0-tensor, a vector a 1-tensor, a matrix a 2-tensor, and a batch of images a 4-tensor. Deep learning is mostly arithmetic on tensors (adds, multiplies, matrix multiplies) because GPUs do these in parallel extremely fast. The shapes matter: a matrix multiply of (m x k) with (k x n) gives (m x n), and most beginner bugs are shape mismatches, so you learn to reason about shapes before values.

The **gradient** of a function is the vector of its partial derivatives: for a loss `L` that depends on a parameter `w`, `dL/dw` tells you how `L` changes for a tiny increase in `w`. If the gradient is positive, increasing `w` increases the loss, so to *decrease* the loss you step `w` in the **negative** gradient direction. That single idea, follow the negative gradient, is gradient descent, the engine under essentially all neural-network training. Everything else (backprop, optimisers) is machinery to compute and apply gradients efficiently.
lessons.tryit: On paper, compute the gradient of L(w) = (w - 3)**2 by hand. Evaluate it at w=5 and at w=3. Confirm the sign tells you which way to move w to reduce L, and that at the minimum the gradient is 0.

questions.prompt: What is a tensor?
questions.explain: A tensor is an n-dimensional array: scalar (0D), vector (1D), matrix (2D), and so on. It is the basic data object, not a network or a loss.

questions.prompt: The gradient dL/dw at the current w is +4. To reduce the loss, how should you change w?
options: Decrease w (step in the negative gradient direction)
questions.explain: A positive gradient means increasing w increases L; to decrease L you move w in the negative gradient direction, i.e. decrease w. This is the core of gradient descent.

questions.prompt: You matrix-multiply A (shape 4x3) by B and get a (4x5) result. What must B's shape be, and why is reasoning about shapes emphasised?
options: 3x5, because inner dims must match and most beginner bugs are shape mismatches
questions.explain: (4x3)@(3x5) -> (4x5): the inner dimensions (3) must match and the outer dimensions give the result shape. Shape reasoning is stressed because shape mismatches are the most common beginner bug.

questions.prompt: L(w)=(w-3)**2, so dL/dw = 2*(w-3). What does this print for the gradient at w=5?
questions.explain: The derivative of (w-3)**2 is 2*(w-3); at w=5 that is 2*2=4. The positive sign says increasing w raises the loss, so descent moves w down toward the minimum at w=3 where the gradient is 0.

lessons.title: Backprop by hand (micrograd)
lessons.objective: By the end you can apply the chain rule to propagate gradients backward through a tiny computation graph.
concept: Backpropagation is just the **chain rule** applied over a computation graph. Build the forward pass as a graph of tiny operations (add, multiply), where each node remembers its inputs and output. To get gradients, start at the loss with `dL/dL = 1` and walk **backward**: each node knows its **local derivative** (how its output changes with each input) and multiplies the gradient flowing into it by that local derivative to produce the gradient for each input. Karpathy's micrograd implements exactly this in ~100 lines, which is why it is the best way to truly understand training.

Two local rules cover most of it. For `c = a + b`, the local derivatives are both 1, so addition **passes the incoming gradient unchanged** to both inputs. For `c = a * b`, `dc/da = b` and `dc/db = a`, so multiplication **routes the incoming gradient to each input scaled by the other input**. When a value feeds into multiple places, its gradients **add up** (the multivariable chain rule). Get these three facts right, +, *, and accumulate, and you can backprop any scalar graph by hand, which is exactly what the project's character-level GPT relies on.
lessons.tryit: Build the graph for L = (a*b) + c with a=2, b=3, c=4. Forward: L=10. Then by hand set dL/dL=1 and compute dL/da, dL/db, dL/dc using the + and * rules. Check: dL/dc=1, dL/da=3, dL/db=2.

questions.prompt: Backpropagation is an application of which rule?
options: The chain rule over a computation graph
questions.explain: Backprop is the chain rule applied node-by-node backward through the computation graph; the other rules are unrelated to gradient propagation here.

questions.prompt: For c = a * b with a=2, b=3, the gradient dL/dc arriving at this node is 1. What are dL/da and dL/db?
questions.explain: Multiplication routes the incoming gradient scaled by the *other* input: dL/da = dL/dc * b = 1*3 = 3, and dL/db = dL/dc * a = 1*2 = 2. Swapping them is the classic mistake.

questions.prompt: Arrange a recursive factorial to represent a tiny computation you could backprop through conceptually.
questions.explain: The header comes first, then the base case test, then its return 1, then the recursive multiply. The base case must be checked before the recursive return, so the ordering is unique.

questions.prompt: A value x feeds into two different multiplications whose gradients back to x are 3 and -1. What is x's total gradient, and why?
options: 2 (gradients from multiple uses add, per the multivariable chain rule)
questions.explain: When a node fans out to multiple consumers, its gradient is the sum of the gradients from each path: 3 + (-1) = 2. You add, not pick or multiply, which is the multivariable chain rule.

questions.prompt: For c = a + b, how does the incoming gradient flow to a and b?
questions.explain: Addition has local derivatives of 1 for each input, so it passes the incoming gradient unchanged to both a and b.

example.code:
a, b, c = 2, 3, 4
L = a*b + c          # forward: 10
# backward (by hand):
dL = 1
dL_dc = dL          # '+' passes grad -> 1
dL_dm = dL          # '+' passes grad -> 1
dL_da = dL_dm * b   # '*' routes * other input -> 3
dL_db = dL_dm * a   # -> 2
print(L, dL_da, dL_db, dL_dc)
example.explain: Forward gives 10; the '+' passes gradient 1 to both m and c; the '*' routes gradient to a (xb=3) and b (xa=2). Prints '10 3 2 1'.

lessons.title: Training loops and loss
lessons.objective: By the end you can describe the four steps of a training loop and why each is needed.
concept: Training a network is a loop over four steps. (1) **Forward pass**: run inputs through the model to get predictions. (2) **Loss**: a single number measuring how wrong the predictions are; for classification this is usually **cross-entropy**, which is low when the model assigns high probability to the correct class. (3) **Backward pass**: backprop the loss to get the gradient of the loss with respect to every parameter. (4) **Update**: nudge each parameter a small step (the **learning rate**) in the negative gradient direction. Repeat for many batches and the loss falls.

One subtlety trips everyone up: in frameworks like PyTorch, gradients **accumulate** across backward passes, so you must **zero the gradients** each iteration, otherwise step N's gradients get added to step N-1's and training diverges. The learning rate is the key knob: too large and the loss explodes or oscillates; too small and training crawls. A healthy run shows the loss decreasing and then plateauing, which is your feedback signal, exactly the engineered feedback from the frontier module applied to ML.
lessons.tryit: Write pseudocode for one training iteration with the four steps, including zero_grad. Then explain in one sentence what goes wrong if you forget zero_grad, and what goes wrong if the learning rate is 100x too large.

questions.prompt: Which is the correct order of the training-loop steps?
questions.explain: You must compute predictions (forward), measure error (loss), get gradients (backward), then adjust parameters (update). No other order makes sense: you can't backprop a loss you haven't computed.

questions.prompt: Your loss decreases for 50 steps then suddenly explodes to NaN. The most likely single cause is:
options: The learning rate is too large, causing updates to overshoot and diverge
The model has too few parameters
questions.explain: A loss that falls then blows up is the classic signature of too-large a learning rate: updates overshoot the minimum and amplify. Dataset size and model capacity don't produce a sudden NaN explosion like this.

questions.prompt: You forget to zero gradients each iteration in PyTorch. What happens and why?
options: Gradients accumulate across iterations, so each update uses a wrong, ever-growing gradient and training destabilises
questions.explain: PyTorch accumulates gradients into .grad by design (useful for gradient accumulation); without zero_grad each step adds to the last step's gradients, producing incorrect, growing updates that destabilise training.

questions.prompt: What does a loss function produce?
options: A single number measuring how wrong the predictions are
questions.explain: A loss is a scalar measuring prediction error; backprop then computes gradients of that scalar.

lessons.title: Neural nets for language: bigram to MLP
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain how a bigram model and an MLP character model predict the next character.
concept: Start as simply as possible. A **bigram** character model predicts the next character from only the current one. You count, in a training corpus, how often each character follows each other character, forming a table of counts; normalising each row to sum to 1 gives next-character probabilities. Sampling from these probabilities generates text that captures local letter statistics (English 'q' is usually followed by 'u') but nothing longer-range, because the model's entire memory is one character.

To do better, give the model **context** and let it **learn** rather than count. An **MLP** (multilayer perceptron) character model, following Bengio 2003 as taught in Karpathy's series, embeds the previous few characters into vectors, concatenates them, passes them through a hidden layer with a nonlinearity, and outputs a probability over the next character, trained by the loss-and-backprop loop from the last lesson. The embeddings let similar characters share statistical strength, and the wider context captures patterns a bigram cannot. This is the conceptual bridge from counting to learned representations that the transformer will extend.
lessons.tryit: Compute a bigram count table for the tiny corpus 'abab'. Write the counts of what follows 'a' and what follows 'b'. Normalise 'a's row to probabilities. Then explain in one sentence why this model can't tell 'abab' from 'abba'.

questions.prompt: What does a bigram character model condition its prediction on?
questions.explain: A bigram model's whole memory is the current character; it predicts the next character from that alone, which is why it captures only local statistics.

questions.prompt: Counting next-character statistics with Counter. What does this print?
questions.code:
from collections import Counter
c = Counter('abracadabra')
print(c['a'], c['b'])
questions.explain: In 'abracadabra', 'a' appears 5 times (positions 1,4,6,8,11) and 'b' appears 2 times. Bigram models are built from exactly these kinds of counts, here simplified to unigram letter counts for the arithmetic.

questions.prompt: Why does an MLP character model generalise better than a bigram count table, given the same corpus?
options: It learns embeddings and uses a wider context, so similar characters share statistical strength and longer patterns are captured
questions.explain: The MLP replaces raw counts with learned embeddings over a multi-character context; embeddings let related characters share evidence and the context captures patterns beyond a single preceding character, which pure bigram counts cannot.

questions.prompt: A bigram model trained on 'abab' assigns what probability to 'b' following 'a'?
questions.explain: In 'abab' every 'a' is followed by 'b' (positions a->b twice), so the normalised probability of 'b' after 'a' is 1.0. The model has no longer context to doubt it.

lessons.title: Attention and transformers
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain self-attention as a weighted lookup and why it beats fixed-context models for language.
concept: The MLP's weakness is a **fixed, small context**. **Self-attention** removes that limit: every position can look at every other position and pull in the information it needs. Each token produces three vectors: a **query** (what am I looking for?), a **key** (what do I offer?), and a **value** (what I'll contribute if attended to). For a given token, you score its query against every token's key (a dot product), turn the scores into weights with a **softmax** (so they are positive and sum to 1), and take the weighted sum of the values. The result is a context-aware mixture: the token has gathered relevant information from the whole sequence.

A **transformer** stacks many such attention layers (plus MLPs and residual connections), using **multi-head** attention so different heads learn different relationships (syntax, coreference, etc.), and in a GPT a **causal mask** prevents a position from attending to future tokens so it can be trained to predict the next token. This architecture, from 'Attention Is All You Need' (2017) and built from scratch in Karpathy's nanoGPT video, is what the project's character-level GPT implements. The softmax weighting is the heart of it: it is how the model decides, per token, what to pay attention to.
lessons.tryit: On paper, write the attention recipe for one query: score q against three keys, softmax the scores, then weighted-sum the values. Use scores [2,2,3] turned to weights, and explain which value dominates and why.

questions.prompt: In self-attention, what are the three vectors each token produces?
questions.explain: Each token produces a query, a key, and a value; a token's query is scored against all keys, and the resulting weights mix the values.

questions.prompt: Attention turns scores into weights that sum to 1. Given these pre-normalised weights [1,1,2], this prints the normalised weights:
questions.code:
ws = [1, 1, 2]
tot = sum(ws)
print([w / tot for w in ws])
questions.explain: Dividing each weight by the total (4) gives [0.25,0.25,0.5], which sum to 1. The third value gets half the attention; softmax does the same normalisation but with exponentials first.

questions.prompt: Why does a GPT use a causal mask during training?
options: So a position cannot attend to future tokens, making next-token prediction a valid, non-cheating task
To remove the need for embeddings
questions.explain: Next-token prediction would be trivial if a position could see the answer (future tokens); the causal mask blocks attention to future positions so the model must genuinely predict. It is about correctness of the training task, not speed or memory.

questions.prompt: What is the role of softmax in attention?
options: It turns raw scores into positive weights that sum to 1, defining how much each value is attended to
questions.explain: Softmax normalises the query-key scores into a probability-like distribution (positive, summing to 1), which weights the values; it is not the loss or the initialiser.

project.brief: Following Karpathy's Zero to Hero, build and train a small character-level transformer on a text corpus of your choice. Every component (backprop, training loop, attention) comes from this module, so you end with a model that generates text and an understanding of why it works.

Build a bigram baseline and record its loss as a reference
Write the training loop with loss, backward, update, and zero_grad; get the loss to fall
Implement single-head then multi-head self-attention with a causal mask
Train the GPT and sample generated text; compare its loss to the bigram baseline

exam.prompt: For c = a*b with a=4, b=5 and incoming gradient dL/dc=2, what is dL/da?
exam.explain: Multiplication routes the incoming gradient scaled by the other input: dL/da = dL/dc * b = 2*5 = 10. Using a instead of b (2*4=8) is the common error.

exam.prompt: Your transformer's training loss won't drop below the bigram baseline. Which diagnosis uses this module's ideas best?
options: Check for a bug: forgetting zero_grad, a learning rate far off, or attention not actually mixing values (e.g. mask wrong)
exam.explain: A transformer should beat a bigram; failing to do so points to a training bug this module names: missing zero_grad, bad learning rate, or a broken attention/mask so values aren't mixed. Blindly adding layers or changing corpus language isn't a diagnosis.

exam.prompt: dL/dw for L=(w-3)**2 is 2*(w-3). What does this print at w=0?
exam.explain: 2*(0-3) = -6. The negative gradient means increasing w decreases the loss, so descent moves w up toward the minimum at 3.

exam.prompt: Connect to the compilers track: both a bytecode VM's fetch-decode-execute loop and a training loop repeat a fixed body. What is the key difference in what each iteration changes?
options: The VM advances an instruction pointer over fixed code; the training loop mutates the model's parameters toward lower loss
exam.explain: Both are loops, but the VM steps deterministically through fixed instructions, while the training loop changes persistent state (parameters) each pass to minimise a loss. The VM computes no gradients.

exam.prompt: What does softmax guarantee about attention weights?
options: They are positive and sum to 1
exam.explain: Softmax outputs a positive distribution summing to 1, used to weight the values.

exam.prompt: A value feeds into three operations with back-gradients 2, -1, and 4. Its total gradient is:
exam.explain: Fan-out gradients add (multivariable chain rule): 2 + (-1) + 4 = 5. You sum contributions, not take the max or product.

exam.prompt: Why is starting with a bigram model before a transformer a good deliberate-practice choice (link to the frontier module)?
options: Bigrams are state of the art
It gives a cheap baseline and immediate feedback, isolating whether added complexity actually helps
Transformers can't be trained from scratch
It avoids writing a loss function
exam.explain: The bigram is a cheap, fast baseline whose loss is immediate feedback; beating it is the signal that your added complexity earns its keep, which is exactly deliberate practice with engineered feedback.

modules.summary: Think like an attacker to defend: threat modeling, memory corruption and its defenses, web exploitation, applied crypto, and a CTF practice method.

lessons.title: Threat modeling
lessons.objective: By the end you can produce a basic threat model by answering the four framing questions for a system.
concept: Security is not a feature you sprinkle on at the end; it starts with **threat modeling**, a structured way to ask what could go wrong before you build. A widely used frame is Shostack's four questions: (1) **What are we working on?** (draw the system and its data flows), (2) **What can go wrong?** (enumerate threats), (3) **What are we going to do about it?** (mitigations), and (4) **Did we do a good job?** (review). The point is to think like an attacker on purpose, systematically, rather than hoping you remembered everything.

To enumerate threats, teams often use **STRIDE**: Spoofing (pretending to be someone), Tampering (altering data), Repudiation (denying an action), Information disclosure (leaking data), Denial of service (making it unavailable), and Elevation of privilege (gaining rights you shouldn't have). You walk each data flow and each trust boundary, the places where data crosses from less-trusted to more-trusted, and ask which STRIDE threats apply. A **trust boundary** (e.g. the line between the internet and your server) is where most real vulnerabilities live, so modeling them explicitly is the highest-value habit. This is defensive work: you model to *defend*, not to attack others' systems.
lessons.tryit: Pick a simple system you know (e.g. a login form backed by a database). Draw its data flow with one trust boundary. Apply STRIDE to the flow crossing that boundary and list one concrete threat per applicable letter.

questions.prompt: What does the 'E' in STRIDE stand for?
questions.explain: STRIDE's E is Elevation of privilege: gaining rights you shouldn't have. Encryption is a mitigation, not a threat category; the others aren't STRIDE letters.

questions.prompt: Where do most real vulnerabilities live, per the lesson, and what should you model explicitly?
options: At trust boundaries; model where data crosses from less- to more-trusted
In the database only; model schemas
questions.explain: Trust boundaries, the lines where data moves from less-trusted to more-trusted (e.g. internet to server), are where most vulnerabilities occur, so modeling them explicitly is the high-value habit.

questions.prompt: A team adds a login feature and asks 'is it secure?'. Which threat-modeling move most improves the answer?
options: Run the code and see if it crashes
Walk the data flow across the internet->server boundary and apply STRIDE (e.g. Spoofing: credential stuffing; Information disclosure: leaking which usernames exist)
Add more unit tests for the happy path
Encrypt the whole database and stop
questions.explain: Systematically walking the trust boundary with STRIDE surfaces concrete, categorised threats (spoofing, info disclosure) you can then mitigate. Crash-testing, happy-path tests, and a single blanket control don't enumerate the threat space.

questions.prompt: What are Shostack's four threat-modeling questions, in order?
options: What are we working on? What can go wrong? What will we do? Did we do a good job?
questions.explain: The four-question frame is: what are we building, what can go wrong, what do we do about it, and did we do a good job.

lessons.title: Memory corruption: overflows and defenses
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain how a stack buffer overflow works and what ASLR, stack canaries, and NX each defend against.
concept: In C, a fixed-size buffer on the stack has no automatic bounds checking. If a program copies attacker-controlled input into a 64-byte buffer without checking length (the classic `strcpy` or `gets` bug), writing past the end **overflows** into adjacent stack memory, including the saved **return address**. Overwrite the return address and you can redirect execution when the function returns. This is the archetypal memory-corruption vulnerability, and understanding it, as a defender, is why it matters: you learn to spot the unbounded copy and reach for bounds-checked alternatives.

Three defenses raise the bar, each against a different step. A **stack canary** is a random value placed between local buffers and the saved return address; the function checks it before returning, so a linear overflow that clobbers the return address also clobbers the canary and is detected. **NX (No-eXecute)** marks the stack non-executable, so even if attackers write shellcode onto the stack, the CPU refuses to run it. **ASLR** randomises where code and stack live in memory each run, so attackers can't reliably know the address to jump to. They are complementary: defeating one doesn't defeat the others, which is why modern systems stack all three (defense in depth).
lessons.tryit: Explain in writing, as a defender, the exact sequence: unbounded copy -> overflow past buffer -> overwrite saved return address -> hijacked control flow. Then match each of canary / NX / ASLR to the step it most directly disrupts.

questions.prompt: What does a stack buffer overflow overwrite to hijack control flow?
options: The saved return address on the stack
questions.explain: Writing past a stack buffer clobbers adjacent stack memory including the saved return address; corrupting it redirects execution when the function returns.

questions.prompt: A stack canary primarily detects which condition before a function returns?
options: That a linear overflow has overwritten the region between buffers and the return address
questions.explain: The canary sits between local buffers and the saved return address; a contiguous overflow that reaches the return address also corrupts the canary, and the pre-return check catches the mismatch.

questions.prompt: An attacker writes shellcode onto the stack and overwrites the return address to point at it. Which defense specifically stops the shellcode from running, and why doesn't a canary?
options: NX marks the stack non-executable so the CPU won't run stack bytes; a canary only detects overwrites of itself, which a precise write might avoid
A canary; it encrypts the stack
questions.explain: NX makes stack memory non-executable, so even a correct jump to shellcode fails to execute. A canary only detects corruption of the canary region and can be bypassed by writes that don't disturb it, so it is not the defense against execution.

questions.prompt: A canary is checked by XORing the stored value with the original; equal values give 0 (OK). What does this print?
questions.explain: XOR of equal values is 0, so an intact canary yields 0 and the check passes. A mismatch (overwrite) would produce nonzero, aborting the program. This mirrors how the canary comparison flags corruption.

lessons.title: Web exploitation: injection, SSRF, auth flaws
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain injection, SSRF, and common auth flaws and the primary defense for each.
concept: Most web vulnerabilities come from **confusing data with code or trust**. **Injection** (SQL, command, etc.) happens when user input is concatenated into an interpreter's instruction: `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name='" + name + "'"` lets an attacker's input become SQL. The defense is not escaping by hand but **parameterised queries / prepared statements**, which send the query and the data on separate channels so the data can never be parsed as code. The same principle, never build code by string-concatenating untrusted input, fixes command injection too.

**SSRF** (Server-Side Request Forgery) tricks your server into making requests it shouldn't, for example fetching an attacker-supplied URL that points at internal services or cloud metadata endpoints. Defenses include allow-listing destinations and blocking internal address ranges. **Auth flaws** are a broad family: broken session handling, missing authorization checks (any logged-in user can access any record by changing an id, an IDOR), and weak password or token handling. The unifying defensive lesson is to validate on the server, enforce authorization on every request, and treat all client-supplied values, ids, URLs, query fragments, as hostile until proven safe. This is defensive knowledge: you learn attacks to build systems that resist them.
lessons.tryit: Take a vulnerable query built by string concatenation and rewrite it as a parameterised query in your language. Then describe, in two sentences, how an IDOR occurs and the one check that prevents it.

questions.prompt: What is the primary defense against SQL injection?
options: Parameterised queries / prepared statements that separate code from data
questions.explain: Parameterised queries send the SQL and the user data on separate channels so input can never be parsed as code. Hiding the DB and password length don't address injection.

questions.prompt: A server fetches any URL a user supplies to 'preview' a link. An attacker submits a URL pointing at the cloud metadata endpoint. This is:
questions.explain: Coercing the server into making an attacker-chosen request to internal/metadata endpoints is SSRF. The defense is allow-listing and blocking internal address ranges.

questions.prompt: Users access /invoice?id=123. Changing it to id=124 shows another user's invoice. Name the flaw and the one fix.
options: IDOR / broken authorization; enforce a server-side check that the current user owns the requested record
questions.explain: Being able to read another user's record by changing an id is IDOR, a broken-authorization flaw. The fix is a server-side ownership/authorization check on every request, not input escaping (the id is well-formed) or network controls.

questions.prompt: What single principle underlies injection, SSRF, and IDOR defenses?
options: Treat all client-supplied values as hostile and validate/authorize on the server
questions.explain: All three stem from trusting client input; the unifying defense is server-side validation and per-request authorization, treating ids, URLs, and query fragments as hostile. Encryption alone fixes none of them.

right.title: Safe (parameterised)
points: Data sent on a separate channel

lessons.title: Crypto done right: don't roll your own
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain why to use AEAD and a key-management discipline instead of building crypto primitives yourself.
concept: The first rule of applied cryptography is **don't roll your own**. Not because you aren't smart, but because secure crypto depends on a thousand subtle details, constant-time comparisons, correct nonce handling, padding, side channels, that have broken experts repeatedly. Instead, use well-reviewed libraries and high-level APIs. For encrypting data you almost always want **AEAD** (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data), such as AES-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305, which provides both **confidentiality** (nobody can read it) and **integrity/authenticity** (nobody can tamper with it undetected) in one primitive.

Why AEAD and not plain encryption? Encryption alone (e.g. AES-CBC without a MAC) hides contents but lets an attacker flip bits that silently change the decrypted plaintext; AEAD's authentication tag makes any tampering a decryption failure. Two disciplines matter alongside the primitive: **never reuse a nonce** with the same key (nonce reuse can catastrophically break AES-GCM), and **key management**, where keys come from, how they're stored (a secrets manager or KMS, not in source), how they rotate. The practical stance: pick a vetted library, use its AEAD API correctly, and spend your real effort on key management, which is where most production failures actually happen.
lessons.tryit: Find your language's recommended AEAD API (e.g. libsodium, Python 'cryptography' AESGCM). Write the three lines to encrypt and decrypt a message with a key and nonce. Then write two sentences on where the key should come from and why nonces must not repeat.

questions.prompt: What two properties does AEAD provide?
questions.explain: AEAD gives confidentiality (secrecy) and integrity/authenticity (tamper detection) together. It is not a compressor, hash, or key-exchange mechanism.

questions.prompt: Why prefer AES-GCM over AES-CBC-without-a-MAC for encrypting a message?
options: GCM authenticates the ciphertext, so tampering is detected; unauthenticated CBC lets attackers alter plaintext silently
questions.explain: The decisive reason is authentication: GCM (an AEAD mode) detects tampering, while plain CBC provides only confidentiality and is malleable, letting attackers change the decrypted result undetected. GCM still requires a unique nonce.

questions.prompt: A developer stores an API key in source and reuses one fixed nonce for all AES-GCM messages 'for simplicity'. Name the two serious mistakes and the better practice.
options: Hardcoded key (use a secrets manager/KMS) and nonce reuse (can catastrophically break GCM; use a unique nonce per message)
questions.explain: Both are serious: a key in source is exposed to anyone with the code and should live in a KMS/secrets manager, and reusing a GCM nonce under the same key can leak the authentication key and plaintext relationships. A unique nonce per encryption is mandatory.

questions.prompt: What is the first rule of applied cryptography per the lesson?
options: Don't roll your own; use vetted libraries and high-level APIs
questions.explain: Don't roll your own crypto: the subtle details break even experts, so use well-reviewed libraries and high-level AEAD APIs.

lessons.title: CTF practice method
lessons.objective: By the end you can run a disciplined CTF practice loop and write a useful challenge write-up.
concept: **Capture the Flag** (CTF) is deliberate practice for security: self-contained challenges (web, binary exploitation, crypto, reverse engineering) where you find a 'flag' by exploiting an intentionally vulnerable target in a legal, sandboxed arena like pwn.college. The value is that each challenge has a definite answer, so you get **immediate feedback**, exactly the engineered feedback the frontier module demands. The discipline is to work at the edge of your ability: pick challenges you can *almost* solve, and when truly stuck, read the hint or a write-up, but only after a real attempt.

The habit that turns CTF hours into durable skill is the **write-up**: after solving (or reading the solution), write down the vulnerability, the exact steps to exploit it, and the general lesson. Writing forces you to understand the mechanism rather than the lucky keystrokes, which is the writing-to-learn effect from the frontier module, and a library of your own write-ups becomes a personal playbook. Always stay inside the rules: CTFs and platforms like pwn.college are explicitly built as safe, legal environments. The method, not raw hours, is what compounds.
lessons.tryit: Pick one beginner pwn.college or CTF challenge in a category you want to improve. Timebox a genuine attempt. Whether you solve it or read the solution, write a short write-up: the vulnerability, the exploit steps, and the general lesson.

questions.prompt: What makes CTF challenges good deliberate practice?
options: Each has a definite flag, giving immediate feedback on whether you succeeded
questions.explain: A definite flag means immediate, unambiguous feedback, the key ingredient of deliberate practice, letting you know at once whether your approach worked.

questions.prompt: You've been stuck on a challenge for an hour with no progress. What does the lesson's method recommend?
options: After a genuine attempt, read a hint or write-up, then make sure you understand the mechanism
Immediately read the full solution before trying
Switch to a much harder challenge
questions.explain: The method is to attempt genuinely at the edge of ability, then use hints/write-ups once truly stuck, and consolidate by understanding the mechanism. Reading the solution first removes the practice; quitting or jumping harder removes the feedback loop.

questions.prompt: Why does writing a CTF write-up build more durable skill than just moving to the next challenge?
options: Writing forces understanding of the mechanism (not lucky keystrokes) and builds a reusable playbook, the writing-to-learn effect
It slows you down on purpose with no benefit
questions.explain: Articulating the vulnerability and steps forces you to understand why the exploit worked, converting a one-off solve into transferable knowledge, exactly the writing-to-learn principle from the frontier module.

questions.prompt: CTF practice should always happen:
options: On any system you find online
Inside legal, sandboxed arenas built for it (e.g. pwn.college)
questions.explain: CTFs are explicitly safe, legal environments; practice belongs there, never against systems you aren't authorised to test.
