exam.prompt: A login endpoint builds its SQL by string-concatenating the username and uses one fixed AES-GCM nonce for session tokens. Which two fixes apply?
options: Parameterised queries; and a unique nonce per encryption
exam.explain: The concatenated SQL needs parameterised queries, and fixed-nonce AES-GCM needs a unique nonce per message. Canary/NX/ASLR are memory-corruption defenses, irrelevant to these two web/crypto flaws.

exam.prompt: An attacker overwrites a stack return address but the exploit fails to run their shellcode even though the jump lands on it. Which defense is most likely active?
exam.explain: Landing on the shellcode but failing to execute it is the signature of NX marking the stack non-executable. The other options are web/crypto controls unrelated to stack execution.

exam.prompt: Using STRIDE, 'any logged-in user can read another user's invoice by changing an id' is primarily which category?
exam.explain: Accessing resources beyond your rights is Elevation of privilege, with Information disclosure as the consequence. It is not impersonation (spoofing), availability (DoS), or deniability (repudiation).

exam.prompt: Connect to the compilers track: a buffer overflow overwrites a return address, and an interpreter bug lets input become code (injection). What single principle links both vulnerability classes?
options: Both arise from failing to keep a boundary between trusted control/code and untrusted data
exam.explain: Overflow lets data cross into control flow (return address); injection lets data cross into code. Both are failures to separate untrusted data from control/code, the same boundary-violation principle, defended by bounds checks and parameterisation respectively.

exam.prompt: What is the first rule of applied cryptography?
options: Don't roll your own; use vetted libraries and AEAD
exam.explain: Don't roll your own crypto; rely on well-reviewed libraries and AEAD APIs.

exam.prompt: Why is a definite flag in a CTF pedagogically valuable?
options: It provides immediate, unambiguous feedback, the core of deliberate practice
exam.explain: Immediate feedback (did I get the flag?) is exactly what deliberate practice needs; it tells you at once whether your approach worked.

exam.prompt: A server-side 'URL preview' feature lets users submit any URL. Beyond blocking it, what is the defensible way to keep the feature per this module?
options: Allow-list permitted destinations and block internal/metadata address ranges (SSRF mitigation)
exam.explain: This is an SSRF risk; the module's mitigation is allow-listing destinations and blocking internal/metadata ranges so the server can't be coerced into internal requests. Encryption and captchas don't address the SSRF.

modules.title: Track: Performance and database internals
modules.summary: Measure first, then exploit the machine: caches and data layout, SIMD, query execution models, buffer pools, and concurrency control.

lessons.title: Measuring: perf and hardware counters
lessons.objective: By the end you can state why you must measure before optimising and name what perf and hardware counters reveal.
concept: The cardinal rule of performance work is **measure first**. Intuition about what is slow is wrong often enough that optimising without data usually wastes effort on code that isn't the bottleneck. Amdahl's law makes this concrete: if a function is 5% of runtime, making it infinitely fast gives at most a 5% speedup, so you must find the part that dominates. A **profiler** attributes time to functions or lines; on Linux, **perf** is the standard tool, able to sample where the CPU spends cycles with low overhead.

Beyond wall-clock time, modern CPUs expose **hardware performance counters**: cache misses, branch mispredictions, instructions retired, cycles. These explain *why* code is slow, not just where. A loop that looks simple but has a high cache-miss rate is memory-bound; one with many branch mispredictions is hurting from unpredictable control flow. Brendan Gregg's work popularised reading these systematically (and visualising with flame graphs). The workflow is: measure to find the hot spot, read counters to understand the cause, change one thing, and **measure again**, which is the deliberate-practice loop with the CPU as your feedback source.
lessons.tryit: Take any small program of yours. Time it, then use a profiler (cProfile in Python, or perf for native code) to find the single hottest function. Write down its share of runtime and, using Amdahl's law, the maximum speedup possible from optimising only it.

questions.prompt: What is the cardinal rule of performance optimisation?
questions.explain: Measure first: intuition about bottlenecks is frequently wrong, so you profile to find where time actually goes before changing anything.

questions.prompt: A function is 5% of total runtime. By Amdahl's law, the maximum overall speedup from optimising only it is:
questions.explain: Even reducing that 5% to zero leaves 95% untouched, so the best case is roughly a 1/0.95 ~ 1.05x speedup. This is why you target the part that dominates runtime, not a minor one.

questions.prompt: Two loops have identical instruction counts, but loop A runs 3x slower. perf shows A has a high cache-miss rate and B does not. What does this tell you?
options: A is memory-bound: it stalls waiting on memory, so the fix is data layout/access pattern, not fewer instructions
questions.explain: Equal instructions but more cache misses means A stalls on memory (memory-bound); the lever is improving locality/data layout, not reducing instructions. Hardware counters reveal this 'why' that wall-clock time alone hides.

questions.prompt: What do hardware performance counters measure that a wall-clock timer does not?
options: Cache misses, branch mispredictions, cycles, and other 'why it's slow' signals
questions.explain: Counters expose microarchitectural causes (cache misses, branch mispredicts, cycles) that explain why code is slow, which a stopwatch cannot.

lessons.title: CPU caches and data-oriented design
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain the cache hierarchy and why data layout dominates performance for data-heavy code.
concept: A modern CPU core is far faster than main memory: an L1 cache hit costs ~1ns, while a main-memory miss costs ~100ns, roughly 100x. The CPU hides this with a **cache hierarchy** (L1, L2, L3) that keeps recently used data close. Crucially, memory is moved in **cache lines** (typically 64 bytes), so when you touch one byte you pull in its 64-byte neighbourhood. Code that accesses memory **sequentially** uses every byte of each line it loads; code that jumps around wastes most of each line and stalls on misses.

This is why **data-oriented design** often beats object-oriented layouts for performance-critical code. Consider updating one field across a million objects: an **array-of-structs** (AoS) interleaves all fields, so iterating one field skips over the others and wastes cache lines; a **struct-of-arrays** (SoA) stores each field contiguously, so the loop streams through exactly the data it needs with near-perfect locality. The lesson generalises: arrange data for how it is accessed. The same principle explains why flat arrays beat linked lists for traversal and why column stores (next lessons) win analytic queries.
lessons.tryit: Estimate: iterating a million-element array of 8-byte values, how many 64-byte cache lines must be loaded? Then describe how changing an array-of-structs (x,y,z per point) to struct-of-arrays changes the lines touched when summing only the x values.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much slower is a main-memory access than an L1 cache hit?
questions.explain: An L1 hit is ~1ns and a main-memory access ~100ns, about a 100x gap; hiding this gap is the whole purpose of the cache hierarchy.

questions.prompt: Summing a small matrix row by row (sequential, cache-friendly). What does this print?
questions.code:
m = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
print(sum(sum(row) for row in m))
questions.explain: Each row is summed (1+2+3=6, 4+5+6=15) and the totals added: 6+15=21. Iterating row by row is the sequential, cache-friendly access pattern the lesson favours.

questions.prompt: You iterate a million points summing only the x field. Why is struct-of-arrays faster than array-of-structs here?
options: SoA stores all x values contiguously, so each loaded cache line is full of needed x's; AoS interleaves y,z and wastes most of each line
questions.explain: With AoS, each 64-byte line mostly holds y and z you don't need, so you waste bandwidth and suffer more misses; SoA packs x contiguously so every loaded line is useful. Total memory is similar; locality is the difference.

questions.prompt: Memory is fetched in units of about:
questions.explain: Memory moves in cache lines (typically 64 bytes); touching one byte loads its whole line, which is why sequential access is efficient.

left.title: AoS [x,y,z, x,y,z, ...]
points: Each cache line mostly y,z you skip

right.title: SoA [x,x,x,...][y,...][z,...]
points: Each loaded line is all x

lessons.title: SIMD and vectorization intro
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain how SIMD processes multiple data elements per instruction and when it helps.
concept: **SIMD** (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) lets one instruction operate on several values at once. A 256-bit AVX2 register holds eight 32-bit floats; a single `vaddps` adds eight pairs in the time one scalar add would take one pair, up to an 8x arithmetic throughput gain. This is **data parallelism** within a single core, distinct from multithreading. Compilers can **auto-vectorize** simple loops, but only when the loop is amenable: no data dependencies between iterations, a predictable stride, and often aligned data.

SIMD helps when the same operation applies uniformly to a large array, summing, scaling, dot products, pixel math, and hurts or doesn't apply when iterations depend on each other or control flow diverges per element (branchy code). To use it you either let the compiler auto-vectorize (write clean, dependency-free loops and check the output), use library routines, or write **intrinsics** for direct control. SIMD multiplies arithmetic throughput, but if your loop is memory-bound (from the caches lesson), you must fix locality first, there is no point feeding a vector unit faster than memory can supply it. Measure to know which regime you're in.
lessons.tryit: Write a scalar loop that sums an array of 8 numbers, then describe how an 8-wide SIMD add would compute the same sum with partial sums in a vector register. Note one property the loop must have for the compiler to auto-vectorize it.

questions.prompt: What does SIMD stand for and do?
options: Single Instruction Multiple Data: one instruction operates on several values at once
questions.explain: SIMD = Single Instruction, Multiple Data: one instruction processes multiple data elements in parallel within a core (data parallelism).

questions.prompt: A SIMD sum would reduce this array; the scalar result is:
questions.explain: range(8) is 0..7; their sum is 28. A SIMD approach would add elements in parallel lanes and then reduce the partial sums to the same 28; the result is identical, only the throughput differs.

questions.prompt: A loop sums an array but is memory-bound (high cache-miss rate). You hand-vectorize it with SIMD and see little speedup. Why?
options: The bottleneck is memory bandwidth, not arithmetic; feeding a vector unit faster than memory supplies data gives no gain until locality is fixed
questions.explain: SIMD multiplies arithmetic throughput, but a memory-bound loop is limited by how fast memory delivers data; vectorizing the arithmetic doesn't help until you fix locality. This is why you measure which regime you're in first.

questions.prompt: Which loop is most amenable to compiler auto-vectorization?
options: One where each iteration depends on the previous result
One with no inter-iteration dependencies, a fixed stride, and uniform operation
One with a different branch taken every element
One that calls a different function per element
questions.explain: Auto-vectorization needs independent iterations, predictable stride, and a uniform operation; dependencies and per-element branching block it.

lessons.title: Query execution: volcano vs vectorized
lessons.objective: By the end you can contrast the volcano (tuple-at-a-time) and vectorized execution models and why vectorized is faster for analytics.
concept: A database turns a query plan into executable operators (scan, filter, join, aggregate). The classic **Volcano / iterator model** gives every operator a `next()` that returns **one tuple** at a time, pulling from its child. It is beautifully composable, you can wire any operators together, but it pays a **function call (and virtual dispatch) per tuple per operator**, and processes data one row at a time, which is cache-unfriendly and defeats the CPU's pipelining. For transactional point queries touching few rows this is fine; for analytics scanning millions of rows the per-tuple overhead dominates.

The **vectorized model** (pioneered by MonetDB/X100) keeps the operator structure but passes **batches** of, say, 1,000 values through each operator's `next()`. Now the per-call overhead is amortised over a whole batch, the inner loops run over contiguous arrays (great locality, often auto-vectorizable with SIMD), and branch prediction improves. This is the data-oriented design and SIMD ideas from earlier lessons applied to query engines: process columns in batches, not rows one at a time. The alternative high-performance approach is **compilation** (generate machine code for the query), but vectorized execution gets most of the win with far less complexity, which is why modern analytic engines use it.
lessons.tryit: Sketch a volcano pipeline scan -> filter -> project as three iterators where each pulls one tuple from its child. Then describe the single change that turns it vectorized, and name two CPU-level reasons the vectorized version is faster.

questions.prompt: In the volcano/iterator model, how much data does each next() call return?
questions.explain: The volcano model returns one tuple per next() call, pulling from child operators; this per-tuple granularity is the source of its overhead.

questions.prompt: Arrange the construction of a volcano-style pipeline: scan feeds a filter, which feeds a projection, which is consumed.
questions.explain: Each operator wraps the previous one's output, so scan must be built first, then the filter over it, then the projection over the filter, and only then can you iterate the final operator. The data dependencies make the order unique.

questions.prompt: A tiny volcano-style filter over a scan generator. What does this print?
questions.explain: scan yields each row; select passes through only rows where x%2==0, i.e. 2 and 4. This is exactly the iterator model: operators chained, pulling one value at a time, materialised here with list().

questions.prompt: Why is the vectorized model faster than volcano for scanning millions of rows?
options: Batches amortise per-call overhead and run tight loops over contiguous arrays (better locality, SIMD-friendly, better branch prediction)
It uses one thread instead of many
questions.explain: Vectorized execution processes batches, so the per-tuple dispatch cost is spread over ~1000 values and inner loops stream contiguous data with good locality and vectorization. It returns the same rows; the win is microarchitectural, applying the caches/SIMD lessons.

points: Call + dispatch per tuple per operator

lessons.title: Buffer pools and concurrency control
lessons.objective: By the end you can explain what a buffer pool does and how two-phase locking and MVCC keep concurrent transactions correct.
concept: A database's data lives on disk but is operated on in memory, so the **buffer pool** is the in-memory cache of disk **pages** that the DBMS manages itself (rather than trusting the OS page cache, because the DBMS knows its own access patterns). When a query needs a page, the buffer pool returns it if resident (a hit) or reads it from disk (a miss), evicting some page to make room using a policy like LRU or clock. **Dirty** pages (modified in memory) must be written back before eviction. This is the same cache-hierarchy idea from the CPU lessons, one level up: keep hot data close, and the hit rate dominates performance.

Concurrency control keeps simultaneous transactions from corrupting each other while preserving **isolation**. **Two-phase locking (2PL)** is the classic pessimistic scheme: a transaction acquires locks in a growing phase and releases them only in a shrinking phase (no new locks after the first release), which guarantees serializability but can deadlock. **MVCC** (Multi-Version Concurrency Control), used by Postgres and others, is optimistic about reads: each write creates a new **version**, and readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers (and vice versa), so 'readers don't block writers'. The trade-off is keeping old versions around and cleaning them up (vacuum). Both aim at the same goal, isolation, by different strategies.
lessons.tryit: Explain the buffer pool in two sentences: what it caches and what must happen before a dirty page is evicted. Then state, in one sentence each, the core promise of 2PL and of MVCC, and name one downside of each.

questions.prompt: What does a database buffer pool cache?
questions.explain: The buffer pool is the DBMS-managed in-memory cache of disk pages; hits avoid disk reads. It caches data pages, not query text or credentials.

questions.prompt: Before a dirty (modified) page can be evicted from the buffer pool, what must happen?
options: It must be written back to disk so the modification isn't lost
questions.explain: A dirty page holds changes not yet on disk; evicting it without writing back would lose data, so it must be flushed first. Clean pages can be dropped freely.

questions.prompt: Postgres lets a long analytic read run without blocking concurrent writers. Which concurrency-control mechanism explains this, and what is its cost?
options: Two-phase locking; cost is extra memory
MVCC; readers see a snapshot via versions so they don't block writers, at the cost of keeping/cleaning old versions (vacuum)
A buffer pool; cost is disk space
questions.explain: Non-blocking readers-vs-writers is MVCC's signature: each write makes a new version and readers use a consistent snapshot. The cost is retaining old versions and reclaiming them (vacuum). 2PL would make the reader take locks that can block writers.

questions.prompt: What does the 'two-phase' in two-phase locking refer to?
options: A growing phase (acquire locks) then a shrinking phase (release), with no new locks after the first release
questions.explain: 2PL splits a transaction into a lock-acquisition (growing) phase and a lock-release (shrinking) phase; forbidding new locks after the first release is what guarantees serializability.

project.title: Build a tiny column store, or speed up a hot loop 10x with SIMD
project.brief: Pick one capstone. Either build a minimal column-oriented store with vectorized scan/filter/aggregate, or take a measured hot loop and make it 10x faster using the caches and SIMD lessons. Measurement is the spine of either path.
milestones: Profile to establish a baseline and identify the true hot spot (and read hardware counters)
For the column store: store columns contiguously and implement a vectorized scan + filter in batches
For the SIMD path: improve data layout for locality, then vectorize the hot loop (auto-vectorize or intrinsics)
Measure again and confirm the speedup with counters, not just wall-clock time
Write up the before/after numbers and which microarchitectural effect produced the gain
project.stretch: Add a simple concurrency-control scheme (2PL or MVCC-style snapshots) to the column store and test it under concurrent readers and writers.

exam.prompt: A loop is 80% of runtime. By Amdahl's law, optimising only it to run 4x faster gives roughly what overall speedup?
exam.explain: New time = 0.2 + 0.8/4 = 0.2 + 0.2 = 0.4 of the original, so speedup = 1/0.4 = 2.5x. The untouched 20% caps the gain below the per-part 4x.

exam.prompt: You vectorize a hot summation loop with SIMD but see almost no speedup; perf shows a high cache-miss rate. What is the correct next step?
options: Fix data layout/locality first (it's memory-bound); SIMD can't help until memory can feed the vector unit
exam.explain: A high cache-miss rate means memory-bound: the bottleneck is bandwidth/locality, so improving data layout comes first. Widening SIMD feeds a unit that's already starved for data.

exam.prompt: Rebuild the volcano pipeline order: scan, then filter, then project, then consume.
exam.explain: Operators wrap their child, so scan is built first, then filter over scan, then project over filter, then iteration of the final operator. Data dependencies force a unique order.

exam.prompt: Connect to the ML and compilers tracks: data-oriented design, vectorized query execution, and bytecode VMs all improve speed. What shared mechanism explains the win?
options: They replace scattered pointer-chasing with flat, contiguous data/instructions the CPU streams through with good locality and amortised dispatch
They all reduce the number of operations
exam.explain: SoA layouts, batched vectorized operators, and flat bytecode all turn pointer-heavy, per-item-dispatch work into contiguous streams with better cache locality and amortised overhead, the same microarchitectural lever.

exam.prompt: What must happen before a dirty buffer-pool page is evicted?
options: It is flushed (written back) to disk
exam.explain: A dirty page's changes aren't yet on disk, so it must be written back before eviction to avoid data loss.

exam.prompt: Which statement about MVCC is correct?
options: Readers don't block writers because each write creates a new version and readers use a snapshot
It eliminates all concurrency bugs for free
It stores only one version per row
exam.explain: MVCC's defining property is that readers see a consistent snapshot via multiple versions, so they don't block writers; the cost is maintaining and vacuuming old versions.

exam.prompt: For a transactional workload of tiny point queries (read one row by key), why might the volcano model be perfectly fine despite being 'slow' for analytics?
options: Per-tuple overhead only dominates when scanning many rows; a point query touches one row, so batching buys little
exam.explain: The volcano model's weakness is per-tuple overhead over huge scans; a point query returns a single row, so there's almost nothing to amortise and its simplicity is fine. Vectorization's benefit scales with batch size.
